newsitem.title: FRANCE: French stocks hit record close, Rhone rockets.
newsitem.headline: French stocks hit record close, Rhone rockets.

text.p: French stocks hit a record closing high on Thursday, with Rhone-Poulenc shares leaping by nearly 20 percent after news that the chemicals and drugs firm planned to buy out its U.S. subsidiary Rhone-Poulenc Rorer.
Traders said cash-rich investors were convinced the market could only go one way -- up -- and the market was benefiting from high liquidity.

Other financial market players also say repayments on the "Balladur" government bond will free up some 90 billion francs held by retail investors and that banks are preparing stock investment offers to tap the new money.
The blue-chip CAC-40 index finished up 26.20 points, or 0.91 percent, at 2,893.64. The CAC-40 future ended up 31.0 at 2,894. It hit an intra-day record high of 2,900.82.
Volume was a hefty 8.3 billion francs for the CAC-40.
The CAC-40 had finished 2.97 percent higher on Wednesday, at 2,867.44.
"This is really the way the market wants to go right now," said one trader. "There's a lot of liquidity and a long way to go to fill the gap on other markets."
Renewed optimism over drug and bank sector restructuring helped fuel the rise, traders said.
Rhone-Poulenc ended 19.16 percent higher at 252.5 francs after 7.95 million shares changed hands.

Rhone said it planned to buy rest of its 68.3 percent-owned RPR for 25 billion francs and it will in any case regroup its chemical and fibres businesses in a single unit that would be partly spun off and listed on the Paris bourse in 1998.
Other pharmaceutical sectors players Sanofi and Synthelabo were helped by Rhone news.
Paribas lead a rise in bank stocks, up 2.63 percent at the close, as the market sensed further restructuring.
The stock was also added to Cheuvreux de Virieu broker's list of recommended stocks, a fund manager noted.

Cap Gemini, down more than five percent at one stage, ended 2.76 percent lower at 335.5 francs after news that Daimler-Benz plans to sell its 24.4 percent stake and end a six-year alliance through its Debis joint venture in Germany.

"On the level of fundamentals, this is good news because it clears up the shareholder situation and gets rid of Cap Gemini's handicap on the U.S. market," said Banques Populaires analyst Didier Orand.
Cap Gemini chief executive Serge Kampf said the firm was now free to pursue U.S. acquisitions and that the alliance had been plagued by strategic and management differences.
The share damage was due to end of speculation that Daimler might take over Cap Gemini.
